subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT OF TARIFF BOARD

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT OF TARIFF BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table copies in English and French of a report which I received yesterday from the chairman of the tariff board. It is the board's report on reference No. 124, fruits and vegetables. The report is accompanied, as is usual, by a transcript of the evidence received by the board at its public hearings.
I know there will be widespread interest in the contents of this report, both on the part of hon. members and on the part of fruit and vegetable growers, processors, and others concerned. For that reason the tariff board, with my approval, gave priority to the completion of this report and a special effort has been made to avoid any delay in tabling it. In that connection I wish to thank my colleague, our gracious Secretary of State (Mrs. Fairclough), for facilitating the prompt printing of the report despite the fact that the Queen's printer was heavily committed on other work.
The tariff board reference arose from the fact that in recent years there had been representations from producers pointing to important changes in techniques of production and methods of distribution, as well as in prices, of fresh fruits and vegetables. It had been suggested that the system of seasonal tariffs was in need of revision. The tariff board was therefore asked to make a study of the items in the Customs Tariff covering fresh fruits and vegetables of a kind grown in Canada and, if such study indicated that amendments to the Customs Tariff were desirable, to prepare a revised schedule of tariff items, with recommendations as to rates of duty. The board was asked also to indicate any consequential amendments which might be required in the tariff items covering the same fruits and vegetables in processed form.
As I have so recently received the tariff board's report, there has not been time for my colleagues and me to make a thorough study of its analysis of the situation and its recommendations as to future action. I am, however, in a position to give the house at
this time some indication of the nature and extent of the proposals contained in the report.
The tariff board received briefs from the Canadian Horticultural Council, processors' representatives, the Canadian Association of Consumers, and others. It held public sittings in Ottawa for three days in July and two days in September. In formulating its recommendations the board appears to have taken account of representations included in the briefs and evidence placed before it at the sittings.
The board's recommendations follow the council's suggestion for the continuation, in principle, of the present statutory provisions for fresh fruits and vegetables. These provisions are intended to give greater protection during the Canadian producers' main marketing season than in the off season. They consist of a basic ad valorem rate of 10 per cent for which may be substituted seasonal specific duties. These seasonal rates have generally a considerably higher ad valorem incidence than the 10 per cent offseason rate. The duration of the application of the in-season rate varies from product to product, depending on the length of the Canadian marketing season.
The tariff board had before it requests from the Canadian Horticultural Council and processors' representatives for 45 changes in the tariff. The requested changes included increases in seasonal specific and other duties, extensions in the periods of application of seasonal duties, the dividing of the application of such duties into two separate periods, and combinations of these forms of tariff protection. The board in its report recommends the adoption in full of the council's proposals in respect of potatoes, asparagus, cauliflower, corn on the cob, lettuce, parsnips, sour cherries, cranberries and prunes. The board further recommends the adoption in part of the proposals in respect of brussels sprouts, cabbage, carrots, celery, cucumbers, mushrooms, onions, peppers, apricots, peaches and pears. Consequential amendments are recommended in the duties on canned and frozen asparagus, frozen brussels sprouts, canned mushrooms, canned apricots, canned and frozen cherries, cranberry jelly or sauce, canned and frozen peaches, and canned prunes.

Inquiries of the Ministry
In its report the tariff board notes that at the public sittings there were suggestions that there should be recourse to the principle of fixing values for duty purposes. The board, however, made no recommendations on this matter, as being beyond its terms of reference.
The Canadian Horticultural Council submitted a request that an additional duty be charged on vegetables imported prepacked in consumer-size polythene or cellophane bags. In making the request the council stated that the bags, if imported alone, would be dutiable at 20 per cent ad valorem whereas for prepackaged vegetables they were dutiable only in so far as they added to the gross weight of the vegetables. Another reason for the request was that the shipping of vegetables in this form led to a greater degree of trimming and preparation, thereby reducing the ad valorem equivalent of the specific duty.
In the light of its study of these representations the tariff board recommended that an item be inserted in the Customs Tariff to provide that an additional duty be charged on certain vegetables when imported during periods of seasonal specific duty in packages weighing five pounds or less. The vegetables to which this provision would apply are green beans, brussels sprouts, carrots, beets, cauliflower, lettuce, peas, parsnips and corn on the cob.
As I have said, the government has not yet had an opportunity to consider the recommendations presented in the report which I have just tabled. I can, however, assure hon. members that the report will be studied carefully, and that the government will give serious consideration to the tariff board's recommendations. If we decide to take action along the lines of these recommendations we would expect to take the necessary steps in conformity with the general agreement on tariffs and trade.

the imports so that the butter price support program will not be affected.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    ENTRY PERMITS FOR U.S. EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour, similar to the previous question I asked on behalf of the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), of which notice has been sent to the minister. Can the minister inform the house whether his department has made any recommendations to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration regarding the length of time covered by the entry permits to be given to American pipeline construction workers who come to this country for the next season's work for Trans-Canada Pipe Lines?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    ENTRY PERMITS FOR U.S. EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his question. The reply is that the Department of Labour has made no recommendation to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration regarding the length of time covered by entry permits to be given to American pipe-line workers who come into this country for next season's work for Trans-Canada Pipe Lines.
The present procedure is that before entry of pipe-line workers from the United States is permitted the Department of Citizenship and Immigration consults the national employment service as to the availability of Canadian workers for the particular jobs. If Canadian workers are available for the jobs in question, then entry of American workers is not permitted. Where there are no qualified Canadian workers for specific jobs, then entry of American workers is permitted.
The entry forms issued by the immigration authorities are temporary permits. The time of each permit assigned varies according to the contractor's estimate of the length of time required to do the job. These estimates are approved by the national employment service. Thus, from this point of view, the national employment service is continually making recommendations as to specific cases and specific jobs, but no general recommendation has been made by the department as such, since none has ever been considered necessary.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON STRIKE OF RIVER PILOTS, KINGSTON MARINE DISTRICT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: STATEMENT ON STRIKE OF RIVER PILOTS, KINGSTON MARINE DISTRICT
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) referred me to a report that three foreign ships had rammed the canal locks at Iroquois, and asked for a further report on the walk-out of the Kingston district pilots.
I am glad to inform the hon. member that the press report to which he referred was apparently erroneous. The canal is continuing to operate and ships are continuing to move through the canal in substantial numbers, although in one or two cases minor damage has been caused to canal walls by ships passing through.
As far as the pilots are concerned, I have again assured their representative that my earlier offer that a scheme guaranteeing them reasonable security of employment would be worked out, if they so desired, still holds good. I also assured them that my officials are prepared to meet with them further at any time to discuss these matters. The district has not been cancelled nor is it intended that the district will be cancelled this autumn, although this course of action was at one stage requested by the pilots themselves.
I have again urged the pilots to return to work, and I understand they are meeting again today to consider their position.

On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Was the minister enunciating government policy when he spoke to the Saskatchewan wheat pool annual meeting in Regina last week and said that farmers should not be expected to provide the storage for surpluses? speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minisier of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when I was speaking to the Saskatchewan pool organization in Regina on Friday I said I was sure that in the house on Monday-I was out by one day-someone would rise and ask me whether or not I had been making a statement of government policy, and my prediction was correct. It is reported in the Leader-Post that the minister made that statement in his speech, and that he also made it in a room in the Saskatchewan hotel to a reporter.
The Fort Garry hotel?

Mr. Speaker, I have the speech here and if I can get the paragraph-

-to which the hon. member is referring

I would be very glad to make them in the house; I have no objection at all.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Let others say it.
Who prepared it?
Which button was pushed?

What I said was based on a reproduction of the speech at Winnipeg of which my hon. friend from the C.C.F. is so enamoured. I used this paragraph there and what I said in Regina was a repetition of it. I was dealing with the general wheat situation, having made a survey of it, and I said: ... it would seem wise to take a long-range view of our wheat problem rather than living just from crop year to crop year. I think it is wrong to consider our surplus wheat production as a millstone around our necks. Rather, we should be deeply grateful that such an abundant food supply is available.
Oh, oh.

I continue:
Canada has been in the wheat business now for two full generations and our wheat production is a permanent feature of our economic history.

This is just one of C.D.'s
old speeches.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Your best speech.
This is a decided improvement upon Liberal policy and Liberal speeches in the past.
At least he used to know what was in them.

Then I went on to say that in times of surplus production it would be wrong to place the whole burden of that surplus carryover on the farmers, and I think it is that to which my hon. friend has referred. It is not right that the farmer alone should bear that burden under circumstances over which he has no control. Consequently I suggested, so far as our top grade wheat supply is concerned, that in times of surplus the nation as a whole should bear a greater responsibility than that of the farmer.

May I ask a supplementary question. Do I take it the minister was just enunciating what had been done by the previous government and not suggesting that some of the burden should be taken off the farmer who has to store so much of his grain on his own farm? I took it from the statement the minister made in his hotel room, as reported in the Leader-Post on the 15th, and also from the report of his speech, that the minister was saying that the farmers should not be expected to provide storage for surpluses. I do not quite understand-
What I am getting at, Mr. Speaker-
Why don't you ask your question?

I have been at pains to point out that the previous government did very little and that we have provided a program that will improve the situation.

I want to know what the government is doing in this regard in addition to what the previous government did. That is what I am asking the minister.

I will enlighten the hon. member. I have what I said here and I shall read it. I went on to say:
Despite the fact that wheat is grown in practically every country in the world, our top grades of Canadian wheat are in a class by themselves and command a premium in the world market. These top grades should be considered a national asset, and, in years of surplus supply, the country as a whole should bear the extra cost involved in storage and carrying charges rather than have that cost become a burden on the farmer. I am glad to receive praise, Mr. Speaker, from my hon. friend who is so knowledgeable with regard to all these problems. The surplus supply of oats and barley has not been quite the problem that we are endeavouring to solve with regard to wheat. Would the minister not say that the carrying charges levied against income from oats and barley is one of the contributing factors to the very difficult position at the present time, in that there is no surplus likely to accrue from the sale of these commodities at present prices?

I take it that there he said, within the last six months-

The price at which wheat is sold to the mills for domestic purposes is the same as the price basis for export, with the exception that on flour sales to specific areas (excluding the United Kingdom, Europe, the United States and its territories and possessions) an adjustment in the purchase price of wheat is granted by the board, to enable Canadian mills to compete with suppliers from other countries in specific flour markets.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. What action does the government intend to take with regard to the importation of United States honey into this country, when we have sufficient honey of our own to supply the Canadian market?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his intention to ask this question. I may say that in the letter accompanying the notice he indicated that he wanted an answer in considerably more detail than the question itself would perhaps call for, and thus I must apologize to the house for the length of the answer which I give.
Official honey production figures for Canada are not yet available, but the 1957 crop is presently estimated at 31,200,000 pounds as compared with 24,272,000 pounds in 1956 and 25,031,000 pounds in 1955.
Imports of honey from the United States into Canada for the first seven months of this year, January to July inclusive, totalled 2,958,741 pounds as compared with 1,590,341 pounds during the same period for 1956. Of this total, almost 2,500,000 pounds entered Canada during the first five months. Despite the increase in imports early in the year, stocks of honey on hand in Canada as at June 30 of this year were about 450,000 pounds less than the stocks on hand at June 30, 1956.
Honey imports during the months of September, October and November, 1956, totalled over 1,200,000 pounds as compared with an unofficial total of less than 300,000 pounds during the period September 15 to November 15, 1957.
Prices paid for bulk honey imported at Toronto are in line with prices quoted by the United States department of agriculture, and the delivered duty paid price is approximately 17 cents per pound, which is the same as the price for domestic honey f.o.b. Toronto. Domestic honey prices have remained practically unchanged for the past year or more.

As there is no indication that either the volume or price of imported honey is depressing the domestic market, no action appears to be warranted or is contemplated at the present time. The department is, however, continuing to watch closely both the volume of imports and market conditions in the United States and Canada.

Mr. Speaker, may I direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Agriculture arising out of a question asked by the hon. member for Selkirk. Can the minister tell us how much Canadian honey was exported in the last two years, specifically to the United States?
Mr. Speaker, this is a question which I think should be on the order paper. Naturally I cannot answer it on the orders of the day without statistics before me.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I agree with the minister. If the minister does not wish to take it as notice, then I suggest the hon. member should put it on the order paper, where it properly belongs.

I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he has any comments on a report which has been received that the Secretary of State of the United States told his weekly press conference that nuclear weapons were now being stockpiled in NATO countries.

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that this question relates to two departments, the Department of National Defence and the Department of External Affairs may I suggest that the Prime Minister be permitted to answer the question.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to a press report this morning Mr. Dulles allegedly made a number of statements. I think I have to refer to those statements in order to answer my hon. friend. The first statement purported to have been made by him is that the United States has nuclear warheads in Canada along with missile bases to back up the early warning radar system. Mr. Dulles went on to say that the United States was studying the possible formation of several stockpiles of atomic weapons in Europe.
Inquiries of the Ministry
When these statements were brought to my attention I could only conclude that Mr. Dulles had been misquoted or misinterpreted. It is interesting to note that a press dispatch has just come in in which Mr. Dulles' statement about warheads being stationed in Canada is somewhat reduced or obliterated. The further statement is made that the opinion was apparently based on information that he received from the Pentagon. Apparently we shall have to wait until we find what Mr. Dulles said before any comment can be made on the question. But in order to make it perfectly clear, I might say that the earlier portion of that statement as to nuclear warheads being stored in Canada has no other basis than the newspaper report.
Mr. Speaker, might I ask a supplementary question of the Prime Minister. Is there any agreement at all between Canada and the United States for the stockpiling of atomic weapons on Canadian soil?
Mr. Speaker, the answer is no.

Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. Does he know of any arrangement, understanding or agreement between Canada and the United States providing for the stockpiling of atomic weapons on Canadian soil?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That question has already been asked and answered today.
On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday, November 14, before I came into the house, the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) addressed this question to the Prime Minister:
May I ask the Prime Minister whether consideration has been given by the government to the removal of the prohibition on the export of defence equipment from Canada to Israel, and if so, what is the result of the consideration?
In reply to that question the Prime Minister on November 14 said:
I think it-
That is the question.
-is of sufficient moment to demand a rather complete reply, and it will be given in due course.
I now give this answer to the question. Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, the export of defence equipment to Israel is only one facet of the broader question of arms export in general, which is under constant

Inquiries of the Ministry consideration and continuous review. The role of the Canadian government in this matter is to receive applications for export permits and to deal with each on its merits.
As regards applications relating to the area in the Middle East in which hostilities occurred last year, there are two governing considerations. First, the United Nations in its resolution of November 2, 1956, recommended, in the light of the military action then taking place in the Middle East, that member states-and I now quote-"refrain from introducing military goods in the area of hostilities". This United Nations recommendation lent international authority to the decision which had already been taken on a national basis by the Canadian government of the time to withhold permission to export to the area any significant military equipment.
It is our view today that developments since the inception of that policy have not been such as to warrant the government in adopting a new policy. We intend therefore to continue to act in conformity with the spirit of the United Nations resolution unless circumstances should dictate a change.
Then there is a second factor which must be kept in mind. In view of the obligations Canada has undertaken through its participation in the United Nations emergency force now stationed on the Egyptian-Israeli frontier, the government is bound to avoid any action which would render more difficult the peacekeeping function of that force or increase the risk of hostilities which might involve its Canadian members. The government is satisfied at the present time that the policy I have described here is the best one and the one that is most conducive toward these objectives.
I would add, Mr. Speaker, that since the decision taken by the government at the end of October, 1956, there have been no shipments of military equipment to Israel. At the time of that decision, permits that had been issued and were still valid were suspended, and no new permits have since been issued.

Mr. Speaker, with reference to the statement made earlier by the Secretary of State for External Affairs I would like to address this question to him. Can the minister tell the house whether any member states of the United Nations have violated or are violating the request of the United Nations not to send military equipment to the Middle East?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will take that question as notice. I am unable to reply adequately at this stage.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED RAILWAY AND ROAD DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, whilst I am on my feet I would like to reply to a question which the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) asked yesterday and which I took as notice, concerning a press report of a statement made by the deputy minister of northern affairs and national resources with regard to the construction of a railway line and roads for the development of certain areas of the Northwest Territories. I have now had an opportunity to read the address to which the report referred and also to ascertain the context in which the remarks were made.
Mr. Robertson, in his capacity as commissioner of the Northwest Territories, was asked by Carleton University to provide the final lecture in a series of four lectures sponsored by the extension division of the university on the subject "The New North". In dealing with the possibilities of future economic development in the north Mr. Robertson stated: "The main factor in the high costs of economic development in the north is transportation" and went on to deal with the inadequacy of present transportation facilities. The particular reference in the press report to which the hon. member

referred is one in which Mr. Robertson stated as follows:
A railway to Great Slave lake will cost about $65 million. It is essential if we are to get anywhere in that region. Basic resource roads to start the development of the area around Great Slave lake and north to Great Bear lake will cost perhaps $20 million.
The statement that the railway is essential is, of course, a statement of opinion. It does not constitute a statement of government policy, but I may say that the government is very much aware of the importance of developing better transportation facilities in the north and, as hon. members know, the two Canadian railways have this summer been jointly undertaking certain investigations into the problems involved in a railway to Great Slave lake.
The hon. member also asked about a reference in the press report that the cost of the railway and of development roads would constitute "a trifling amount relative to the national wealth to be expected in this region". The statement, as reported in these terms in the press report, does not represent the actual text of Mr. Robertson's remarks. Referring to the figures of $65 million and $20 million Mr. Robertson said:
These are substantial figures-but proportionately they are a trifle compared with the public cost of the C.P.R. that was assumed by 3,000,000 Canadians in 1885.
The population figure should actually have been 4,500,000. However, this does not affect the point. The point Mr. Robertson was making was that while $85 million constitutes a substantial amount, it is not nearly as large in relation to the population and wealth of Canada in 1957 as was the public portion of the cost undertaken by a much smaller and poorer population in 1885 in relation to the construction of the C.P.R. I am advised that the value of cash and land subventions to the C.P.R., in 1957 dollars, amounted to $71 per capita in 1885. The costs Mr. Robertson mentioned amount to $5 per capita.

subtopic: FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY
FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the amendment moved yesterday by this group asks that under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act money should be made available without delay to any province that has a hospital plan in operation. As has already been pointed out, this is of great importance to at least three provinces in this country at this time. The thing that disturbed me in the discussion yesterday, having in mind the historic attitude of the Conservative party toward the whole problem of health insurance and hospitalization insurance, is that there is a growing body of evidence that the government is now attempting to evade, to postpone-

subtopic: FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY
speechtext: How silly can you get?

subtopic: FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY
speechtext:
-and to retreat from the attitude and the position it took during 1957 both in the house and in the recent election.
[Mr. Diefenbaker.I
As evidence for that statement I refer first of all to what has already taken place during this session, when there was a discussion as to the interpretation of the words "in force" and "in operation". Only last evening did we get a categorical statement from the minister that when six provinces have acts on their statute books in force, in the sense that they have been proclaimed the law of the province, those provinces that have plans in fact in operation will then be eligible for payments. After its initial retreat the government, by that statement, seems to have come up at least to the position taken by the previous administration.
But I am going to point out that this is a long way from the position taken by that party in the house during the session just before the election. How strongly, vigorously and adequately did so many leading members of the opposition of that day appeal to the government of the day that money under this scheme and under a hospitalization scheme should be made available immediately to any province that had a scheme in operation, even though there should be only one province. At that time the official opposition went so far as to move an amendment asking that that be done. Today the government is not only not prepared to make money available immediately to a province or group of provinces that have schemes in operation, but they are asking that the act be left as it has been, with the result that at least six provinces must have legislation in force on their statute books.
There is another instance in which the Conservative party has retreated a great distance from the stand it took in the house last spring and during the election. I refer, of course, to the strong plea and categorical statement made that people in mental institutions and in tuberculosis sanatoria should be covered under this act by making the provinces eligible for payments on their behalf. That position was taken by leading members of the Conservative party, and in the statements they made in the house last spring they left no doubt as to their position.
The Minister of Finance, who in those days at any rate was noted for direct and forthright statements, had this to say on that point as recorded on page 3381 of Hansard of April 10, 1957. In speaking on a motion to refer back to the committee, he said:
I put before the house the ground that there can be no justification in good sense or in principle or in humanity or in the existing facts of life as applied to the financial difficulties of the provinces and municipalities of this country, for this government to try to drive a wedge between general hospitals on the one hand and tuberculosis hospitals and sanatoria and hospitals and institutions for the mentally ill on the other hand.

That was a very strong statement by the present Minister of Finance. He went on to say:
I ask the house, therefore, to send this back in order that this clause, unworthy of the Canadian parliament, unworthy of the pretensions of the government that this is a comprehensive scheme, should be reconsidered and that its shortcomings should be remedied and that the scheme should in fact be made what the minister improperly pretends it to be, a comprehensive scheme of hospital insurance.
Surely those words are just as true now as they were on April 10. Surely they are much more pertinent today than they were on April 10, since the hon. member who used those words is now on the treasury benches and in a position to make moneys available, and as a member of the government is in a position to have the legislation amended so that tuberculosis sanatoria and mental hospitals can be included under the act.
At that time the hon. member for Eglinton was not speaking as an individual member of the Conservative party. He was not speaking on his own initiative. He in fact was stating party policy because, shortly after making his statement, he was supported by no less a person than the present Prime Minister. The Prime Minister of today, the leader of the opposition of that time, had this to say as recorded on page 3386 of Hansard of April 10, 1957:
This legislation which is designed to bring about the beneficial results which were pictured in such lucid language by the minister just before the dinner adjournment should not remain incomplete by denying to these institutions equality with the hospitals qualified under this legislation. The legislation as it is in its present form, beneficial as it will be, acceptable as it is to members in all parts of the house, is a step in the right direction. But the goal that all of us have in mind will not be achieved until the two types of institutions to which I have made reference are included within the provisions of this legislation.
I ask why the government has not provided legislation at this session to amend the act so that mental hospitals and tuberculosis sanatoria can be included. That was part of the position taken by the Conservative party in the house at the last session. It was not, I may say, a position inconsistent with the stand taken by the Conservative party during the election. It was not a position confined only to this house. As a matter of fact it was a position that was enunciated in the election campaign itself. The hope and the promise were held out to the people of Canada that a Conservative government would correct this very serious omission.
I have in my hand a report taken from the Winnipeg Tribune of May 14 of this year referring to a statement made by the Prime Minister. It is in these words:
The Conservatives, he said, would repair a "serious omission" in the federal health plan 96698-82J
Health Insurance
which does not include tubercular and mental institutions.
Then, as if to underline that statement and to show that it was a correct statement, the Toronto Globe and Mail of May 28 of this year carried this further report under the date line of Saskatoon, May 27. It is as follows:
Noting that the Canadian Hospital Association was meeting in a nearby hotel, Mr. Diefenbaker reminded that the Conservative party had consistently advocated health insurance.
The main reason that the plan is so far advanced today, he added, is because Ontario's Premier Frost, a Conservative, forced the federal government to place it on the agenda of the 1956 federal-provincial conference.
Mr. Diefenbaker said the Conservative party still believes that hospital insurance should cover patients in mental and tuberculosis institutions.
I ask if the government still believes this statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). Does the government intend at this session to fulfil its very definite commitments to the electorate of this country? Are we to take it now that the Conservative party is in power this definite commitment is going to be relegated to the waste paper basket, the same as similar promises have been relegated over so many years by the previous administration?
Well, Mr. Speaker, we in this group are consistent in the attitude we have taken towards national health insurance. We believe in an over-all national health insurance program, but we are interested in the meantime, before that time arrives, in getting the government to act by proceeding as rapidly as possible. We are suggesting by this amendment that payments should be immediately available to any province that has a scheme in operation. In the field of hospitalization insurance Saskatchewan has led all the provinces in Canada. As far back as 1947 the government of Saskatchewan provided an over-all system of hospital insurance for the people of that province. I can well remember the hopes of the members of the government of that day, namely that the federal government would provide for an over-all health insurance program whereby the people of Saskatchewan could obtain money under that legislation.
Saskatchewan has waited now for over ten years. According to the attitude of the government we are going to have to wait a further period of time before any moneys are paid into our hospitalization plan. The plan has already cost the people of Saskatchewan from 1947 to 1956 a total of $147 million. The people of Saskatchewan believe the federal government had a responsibility in this field over those years. They believe that they have been shortchanged by approximately $70 million by

Health Insurance
the governments in office during that time. They do not look kindly on the suggestion that they are going to have to wait another year; that in 1958 they will be denied, under the probable effect of this legislation, as much as $10 million or $11 million for their hospitalization plan.
I suggest that during this session the government should amend the act in keeping with the statements of the Conservative party when in opposition and provide that any province with a plan in effect could immediately obtain its share of the money provided by the federal government for such a scheme. The premier of Saskatchewan is on record many times in this regard. According to the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of May 14 he made a statement that Saskatchewan was disappointed in the attitude of the government because it appeared certain that money would not be available for at least another year. The people of Saskatchewan believe that they have been short-changed; that they should not have to wait another year. They did not agree with the attitude of the former government that under the provisions of this legislation six provinces must have a scheme in force before federal moneys would be available. What does that mean? It means that one province, the sixth province, could hold up moneys going from the federal treasury to the provinces that are prepared to implement such legislation. If Prince Edward Island were the sixth province I can understand there would be a tremendous amount of pressure that might be brought to bear on such a government to provide legislation, since they would be the roadblock preventing moneys from being paid under such an act as this to the five provinces that had systems in operation.
I do not believe any province should be placed in such a position. I do not believe the provinces themselves want to be placed in that position. I think the premiers of the various provinces, in any event the great majority of them, agree with the premier of Ontario that money should be made available immediately to any province that has a system in operation. I make a plea to the government that in this session they introduce legislation to amend the act along lines suggested in the amendment now before the house, that any province including the province of Saskatchewan shall immediately be entitled to money from the federal treasury. I think that is a stand that is consistent with the stand of the Conservative party. I think it is a stand that is consistent with the stand taken by the premier of Ontario. I think it is a stand that is supported by all logic and all reason. I suggest it is a stand

which will lead to the earlier implementation of a national health insurance plan.
We know that when you say there must be six provinces with plans in force and that within those provinces there must be a majority of the population of this country you delay the time at which federal moneys can go to the provinces and hence delay the time when the people in many of the provinces will have a hospitalization plan in operation. In other words this provision in the act, as the members of the opposition in the previous parliament earlier this year so ably pointed out, was placed there as a means of stalling, postponing; a method of delay and procrastination. The same arguments that applied to these provisions relative to the hospitalization insurance are equally valid relative to national health insurance. I suggest that not only should the federal government be prepared to pay money to a province that has a hospitalization plan in operation, but the federal government should be prepared to pay money to those provinces that might wish at this time to embark on a system of comprehensive health insurance. I am convinced in my own mind of this, although I have had no consultation with any member of the Saskatchewan government, that if the federal government would make moneys available immediately to Saskatchewan under this act Saskatchewan will not use those moneys as a method of saving money for some other department in its budget.
Rather Saskatchewan is more than likely to say, "Now we have an opportunity to expand our own health program in Saskatchewan and to include other important health services, and this money now available from the federal government will allow us to provide a more adequate system of health care for the people of Saskatchewan".
I know that there are in this country forces which are opposed to health insurance. In the mail just today we as members of parliament have received a statement by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in which they state they are opposed, directly and definitely, to a national health insurance program. I do not think they speak for Canadians generally. I do not think they reflect in any way the spoken word of the Conservative party over the last number of months. I suggest that the government should pay no attention to these people. I suggest that the government, instead, should maintain the faith of the Canadian people in the commitments and the statements it made, both in this house and during the election campaign, by proceeding now to include mental hospitals and sanatoria in

the provisions of this act and to make moneys under this act immediately available to any province that has a system in operation and to proceed quickly towards the time that Canada shall have a national health insurance program that I believe is supported by the vast majority of Canadians at this time.

subtopic: FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the bells rang yesterday afternoon to summon us to this house, I confess that I came in trepidation for I had been forewarned that the supply motion which was to be introduced would give way to a freewheeling debate in which the opposition might raise any number of subjects. Of these we would have no advance warning. We now know that we are launched into a debate on health insurance. As I sat last night and listened with some degree of affection to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), who was in fact speaking on the first occasion when I came into this house as a spectator, I must confess that my mind went back to that afternoon early in March, 1939 when, as an under-graduate university student, I came to Ottawa. I remember the scene very well. This morning I went to the library to consult references and to check my recollections of what happened. Mr. Speaker, on that afternoon of March 6, 1939, as reported at page 1573 of Hansard of that year, one of the hon. members who is now in this chamber moved:
That in the opinion of this house, the government of Canada should try to secure amendments to the British North America Act, to provide periodical health examinations and provision for suitable treatment for all those suffering from disease.
That was, Mr. Speaker, in 1939. What did the hon. member say about his motion? He said this:
I know the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) will give it his fatherly approval just as soon as the means are at his disposal.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who introduced that motion on March 6, 1939 was the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) who again today sits in this house, 18 years later, and listens to demands for immediate action on health insurance.

subtopic: FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY
speechtext: Thank you.

subtopic: FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY
speechtext:
What answer did the minister make? Later in the day as I sat in the spectators' gallery the then minister of pensions and national health said this as reported at page 1587 of Hansard of March 6, 1939:
This and similar resolutions that have been placed on the order paper during past years-I
Health Insurance
may say in increasing numbers in more recent years-indicate that the people of this country are more and more taking an interest in public health, and so far as I am concerned that is absolutely all to the good. . . .
There has come to a very large number of people in this country the belief that every citizen is inherently entitled to as much right to protection from sickness and disease as to protection from the more violent, if often less hazardous, attacks of those who wish to steal his property or injure his person. ... I believe we have placed behind us the view held in days gone by that sickness, disability and illness were each man's individual concern.
I have been quoting the Liberal minister of pensions and national health of that day, as reported in Hansard. On that day in March, 1939, the hon. member for Fort William was seconded by another member who recalled that he had in fact introduced a resolution on health insurance in this house in 1931. That was one of the predecessors of the present hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Deniset).

subtopic: FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY
speechtext: That was Doctor Howden.

subtopic: FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY
speechtext:
He then on April 27, 1931 introduced a motion in this house:
That, in the opinion of this house, a measure of federal state medicine would be in the best interests of the Canadian people.
He went on to say this:
If the greatest need of the state is health, then the greatest effort of the state should be directed towards securing the health of its people. Surely the provision of an adequate measure for the control and direction of the health of the Canadian people would be in the best interests of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, on February 16, 1928, one of the predecessors of the present hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)- I refer to Mr. Heaps-introduced in this house a motion:
That, in the opinion of this house, the committee on industrial and international relations be authorized to investigate and report on insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity.
He said this:

Mr. Speaker, it seemed to me a paradox when I heard the former minister of health get up in the house last night and, with almost impassioned oratory, cry out that the hospital insurance plan should be instituted without delay.
However, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) at least realizes that, today, all emergency cases at least in the province of Ontario, and I would say across Canada, are admitted to hospital. No one can be denied hospital care under the public health acts of the various provinces. A great number of people, the majority of people, are covered at the present time by one plan or another of hospital insurance.
Naturally my hon. friends across the floor should realize that the crying need across Canada today is for hospital beds; many people have to wait a week to six weeks or even more to get admission; many of these cases require surgery, some have conditions that worsen as time goes on, and for many who suffer malignancy, which accounts for one in eight of all deaths, delay in admission to hospital may make the difference between recovering or receiving treatment too late.
I was interested to check up on the waiting list of one group of practitioners, and I found that of those waiting for admission
[Mr. Brassard.)
for surgery or medical care over 70 per cent were fully covered in respect of the necessary treatment. Some of them would likely have to take rooms and services less costly than those they were paying for, because of their inability to get the service for which they were paying. The great majority of patients on these waiting lists have been waiting a month or more for admission because there were no hospital beds available to accommodate them.
This then, is the plight of the Canadian people and of the doctors who are looking after them. We need more hospital beds, which means more ward beds, more semiprivate rooms and more private rooms.
Mr. Speaker, I think you will agree with me that it has been borne out by experience that under any general comprehensive insurance scheme there will be a sharp increase in the number of beds required as soon as a hospital plan becomes effective. No one will deny this. Where will these beds come from? In my opinion, for the proper care of the sick today we need a realistic building plan which will lead to the provision of the necessary hospitals together with beds and equipment, to meet this problem. The municipalities today find themselves in no position whatever to finance such an undertaking because over the years more and more money has been taken from them by both levels of government.
We also need more out-patient diagnostic services to save hospital beds for people who are really ill. In other words, we need to curtail our admissions to hospitals in the case of those who with proper facilities could be treated as out-patients. Free diagnostic outpatient services would be of prime importance in treating diseases in incipiency, and in protecting patients from morbidity, long hospitalization or even, perhaps, mortality. This has been well recognized by our governments, as shown by the provision across the country of travelling health clinics which provide X-ray examinations free of charge.
I am concerned about costs. As I understand it, I regard Premier Frost's original ideas on hospitalization as being very sound, when he included those who for health reasons could not purchase any plan and those older people who did not have the wherewithal to pay for one. I think this plan would have been a good staircase on which to build, step by step, a full plan. But this, I think, was refused by the previous Liberal government on the grounds that it must be all or nothing.
Costs are an important factor in any plan. Roughly, as I understand it, the cost of hospitalization would be covered by payment of

one-third from the insured, one-third from the federal government and one-third from the provinces. In the records of most provinces which I have been able to check, hospital costs have been doubling about every eight years. The economy has been advancing at the rate of about 35 per cent over the same period of time. Even in Saskatchewan, where they have a health plan which is quoted as one of the most successful, costs have doubled in less than eight years.
Let me say this. Hospital beds must be provided, and must be provided at the federal and provincial levels because of the inability of the municipal taxpayer to accept any more on his already over-taxed shoulders. This fact must be recognized. All this must be added to our consideration of any hospitalization plan, because beds are the first necessity and must be available before any plan can be successfully carried out. I realize that grants are now being made, but these are totally inadequate to supply those beds.
Therefore, in conclusion let me say that anyone who feels that all this can be done in a few months or in a few days is not facing the facts, and I doubt very much if those beds can even be provided as early as the date the premier of Ontario has set. Provision of these facilities must be an integral part of all discussions, and it must be agreed on by federal and provincial governments before any plan of health insurance can be effective.

maintopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION- PROTEST AGAINST "THE PLOUFFE FAMILY" PROGRAM
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION- PROTEST AGAINST "THE PLOUFFE FAMILY" PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the rules of the house are such that they provide me with this opportunity of stating a grievance and of voicing a complaint which has been made to me by a large number of people-of the very best people- of the constituency I represent. This grievance has to do with a television program carried over the French network of the C.B.C. under the title La Famille Plouffe (The Plouffe Family).
I wish to go on record as being in favour of state control of radio and television. The control we have in this country is far from perfect. Being a human institution, the C.B.C. certainly deserves the severe criticism we have to level at it on a number of scores. Yet how much worse things could be if the

only guarantees we enjoyed in this regard were provided by a syndicate of private interests actuated by no other motive than making money.
In spite of its failings, its mistakes, its slowness in getting things done or in reacting, its sins of omission or commission, the C.B.C. has nevertheless, on occasion, given evidence of its good faith. It is precisely because I believe in the good faith of the officials of that organization, then, that I would like to lay before the house a very unfortunate situation which they will no doubt set about to correct. Moreover, any sustained and persevering effort on the part of the Canadian taxpayer would make it possible to bring about the improvement and even the disappearance of certain programs which, in their present form, are far from being acceptable. Among these is La Famille Plouffe. What is the explanation for the fact that a writer who is not devoid of talent, and actors who should show some respect for their public, lend themselves to the presentation of scenes which are so definitely improper, off-colour, slanted and at times immoral and degrading.
I am no prude. I do not believe in going about this world of men with my eyes shut. I know that evil exists, that it has always existed ever since the unfortunate lapse of Adam and Eve, and that we are all exposed to it. But is that sufficient reason to display evil for all to see, to give it the appearance of acceptable and even commendable behaviour, and often to surround it with enticing artifice which tends to allay or dispel the natural repulsion it should induce? Anyone who has the responsibility of raising a family and who takes this duty seriously, will sometimes wonder what attitude to take towards his children when such scenes come into the home, almost forcibly, and violate its privacy. For want of a better explanation, teen-agers can be told that the TV set should remain off at those hours-I would call them tragic hours-or some attempt can be made to make them understand the impropriety and the utter stupidity of certain scenes. But what can you say to children of six, eight or perhaps ten? How can you reason with them? How can you explain those scenes to them? How can you let them play with fire and pretend they do not risk getting burned?
Therefore, as taxpayer and head of a family, and for the sake of moral rights and education, I must protest against the bad taste and insanity of certain episodes of that program: the trip to Florida, the paternal benediction, the visit to hell, the flagpole sitting, the sunbathing on the roof, all of them scenes in which the censor could have made wholesale cuts.
C.B.C.-Program "The Plouffe Family"
As member for Beauce county, however, I have another protest to make here. In the same program, impudence is carried to the point of trying to make the population believe that the flightiness and the vulgar manners of a certain character are representative of the degree of education and the behaviour of the population of one of the most beautiful counties of the province of Quebec. This disgusting type of propaganda has reached such proportions that a large American magazine, in its issue of November 4, felt it should give publicity to that character's reputation and thus give colour to an inaccurate and altogether unfair representation of the lives of the people whom I am very proud to represent in my country's parliament.
Let Mr. Lemelin, the author, and Uncle Gedeon, the actor, labour under no delusion. In Beauce county, in the province of Quebec, we have kept the fine tradition of the paternal blessing on New Year's day and, for my part, I am proud to continue that sacred tradition in my own home, but that benediction is not given in the stable, among the cows. There are some people from Beauce who, no doubt, go to Florida during the winter but it is no lustful junket requiring personal priming up with pep pills. In Beauce county, people still believe in the dogma of hell, and still have enough faith to pray God that those who deride us on television be spared from hell-fire. In Beauce county, as elsewhere, but not more than elsewhere, immorality sometimes makes unfortunate victims, but even they have enough sense of decency to try to hide instead of lying in full view on the roof or verandahs.
No, let Uncle Gedeon go astray, as he himself claims to be doing, on TV or elsewhere in Montreal, but let him take care that, in doing so, he does not go to the dogs for good. Let him keep on spitting on the floor, and puff on his big curved pipe as he talks to the womenfolk, with his hat pulled down over his ears, and do it all, I must say, with amazing naturalness; he can let or induce Time magazine to write, and I quote:
Impersonating a farmer from backwoods Beauce county, he has become Quebec's top nightclub and TV star.
At least I hope he will not have the public believe that the scenes he is interpreting and the degree of education he displays faithfully portray the way of life in the wonderful homes, and worthy population of the constituency of Beauce. And it is as a representative of Beauce that I wish to protest tonight with all the vigour I can muster.

Unemployment
Let the C.B.C. put a stop to these sordid, false and monstrous displays.
If Uncle Gedeon were a genuine native of Beauce, if he actually had spent the main part of his life in that riding, instead of just happening to live for a few years in a nearby parish, he would have learned to know us as we are, and would realize that the part he plays in that program is a travesty of truth and an insult to our people. He would also know by now that our good housewives, our good mothers of Beauce county do not leave rags that have become useless lying around the house, but just throw them into the fire.
Let the C.B.C. do likewise! If it is possible to correct the gross errors of this program,- which otherwise contains much that is good, -it should be done, so that something new and clean, genuine and honest may be shown.
If that cannot be done, let the program be scrapped, and the sooner the better.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that the subject that I wish to introduce at this time this evening was not cleared with the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). In his public statements, particularly the one made at the great convention of the Conservative party in Ontario, the Prime Minister said that for members of parliament to speak about unemployment is to lead the country into a fear complex that could lead to a depression. If the country is being led into a fear complex it is because the Conservative party is in power and we have no responsibility for bringing that about. One statement made by the Prime Minister has appeared in almost all of the papers in identical words. I believe this came from the Gazette. The Prime Minister said:
We do Canada no good, the free world no good, in conveying a false impression which might have the effect of panicking the Canadian people into a depression.
He continued:
There are no words to express what I think of those who, for political purposes, endeavour to talk the Canadian people into a complex that might bring about the realization of their fears.
I am sure that all of us are quite aware of the fact that the Prime Minister is never short of words, and if he has words to describe that situation I wonder why he did not use them in the spring of 1954 when the

Conservative party vied with the C.C.F. party for the opportunity to move an amendment deploring the fact that the then Liberal government were not taking steps to alleviate a serious unemployment situation. This was in the spring of the year when the unemployment situation was becoming less apparent and work was becoming available. As I have said, they did vie with the C.C.F. party and the Conservative party was able to get the floor ahead of the C.C.F. and the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fair-clough) moved an amendment. This amendment was discussed for about a week and during the course of the discussion the Prime Minister spoke for his full 40 minutes. If anyone was attempting to create a fear complex it was the Prime Minister who was then the hon. member for Prince Albert. But what a change in concept; what a change has taken place in his thinking since that time.
After speaking, as I have said, for about 40 minutes, this is the way the Prime Minister wound up his speech. He was endeavouring to get the then prime minister to express the opinion that there was a very serious unemployment situation in Canada. He kept prodding; he took every conceivable method to try to get the government of the day to indicate that there was a very serious unemployment situation. I quote from Hansard of March 15, 1955, at page 2039, where the present Prime Minister, obviously speaking to the then prime minister, said:
Will he not state that he realizes that if we continue to deliberately delude ourselves concerning the unemployment situation we shall bring about a fear complex in this country which will have serious results in the future?
If that is not a direct and absolute reversal of thinking for his own political purposes I should like to know what it is? I have heard the term "Honest John" used rather loosely over there. I do not think we should hear that too often again. What did he offer in the way of a solution to the problem? It was rather nebulous, but here is one rather important suggestion.
What is the grievance?
Unemployment.

Does the hon. gentleman not consider the fact that there are 300,000 unemployed today and that we are facing the possibility of having some 700,000 to 800,000 unemployed this winter, with the government obviously not taking any action whatever, a serious situation?
One would never know what your grievance was until this moment.
Whether or not the minister calls it a grievance is for him to decide.
