With the hon. member
mumbling in his beard it is difficult to know what he is saying. This is the remedy the then hon. member for Prince Albert had at that time:
Professor J. K. Galbraith, professor of economics at Harvard, advocated reductions in personal income tax as a means of restoring a weakened economy. I believe that there must be a reduction in taxation. Today, company taxation is placing too great a load on initiative and in addition is taxing Canada out of the markets of the world.
The throne speech says that there is to be a tax reduction. We hope it will be brought in soon and that it will have the desired effect that the Prime Minister hopes for. Of course, the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) also had some suggestions at that time. Perhaps he went a little bit farther than did his colleague. I quote from Hansard of January 14, 1955. By the way, this was not in the same debate but it is quite obvious from this quotation that the then members of the opposition spent much of that session spreading fear and gloom. He said, as reported at page 218 of Hansard:
I believe the government would do well to study the program about to be undertaken by the government of the United States.
He suggested that we undertake a large road-building program and went on to say:
I am not suggesting for one moment that the government should embark upon a highway-building program.
He did suggest that the government should advance large sums of money to the provinces to carry on such a program. Then, he went further and said:
The government should also provide employment for many thousands of Canadians for several years ahead by making it possible for more people to buy new houses.
He had another good suggestion with respect to the purchase of new homes. He thought that the amount of the down payment should be reduced from 15 per cent to 10 per cent. That is certainly a remarkable suggestion and the minister is in a position where he can make the recommendation. He had some further recommendations. As a matter of fact, there was no end to his recommendations to the government as to what could be done to alleviate the unemployment situation.
Unemployment
But it was not only the members of the Liberal party who began to note that a serious unemployment situation was developing. Innumerable representations have been made to us and every day the newpapers are indicating what the situation is. Unemployment insurance commission officials apparently have discussed the matter with certain officials of the Canadian Congress of Labour. In that regard I should like to refer to a report in the Toronto Star of October 18. It refers to a Mr. Gargrave who, I hesitate to say, is a member of the political education committee of the steelworkers' union, I believe. Apparently he had a discussion with unemployment insurance commission officials and they indicated to him that unemployment may reach as high as 900,000 this year.
I have a letter here from the construction and general labourers union of Vancouver,
B.	C., dated October 15, 1957, the day after the house opened. The letter is signed by
C.	H. Savage, secretary-treasurer, and reads in part as follows:
We would therefore request you to put the unemployment situation on your agenda for a thorough discussion as soon as parliament opens. May we say that our officers are besieged daily by men in search of employment-*
Should we not have met the wishes of this construction union? Should we have gone to the Prime Minister in confidence and whispered to him very carefully that there is a serious unemployment situation in British Columbia? Some of the British Columbia papers are becoming quite concerned about the attitude of the government with regard to the unemployment situation. They are urging that the government face up to the situation rather than try to sweep it under the rug.
British Columbia may be particularly hard hit. As to that, I do not know. I do know that the revenues of the province from the forest industry have dropped by 30 per cent. One-third of the revenues of the province come from the forest industry. It has been hinted by some columnists writing in British Columbia newspapers, men who are very close to the government at Victoria, that there is a possibility of an increase in the sales tax in order that the government may carry on. That would be disastrous because our industries are already hard hit by a 5 per cent sales tax and other general taxes which are having the effect of driving industries out of the province.
We hope that some action will be taken soon to alleviate the situation. It was pointed out the other day that some 1,400 men have been laid off at Kitimat. There is also the danger of the Britannia mine closing down which will put approximately 800 more men out of work. Then there is the construction

Unemployment
industry which has already explained its position and the forest industry where there is approximately a 30 per cent reduction. These are very serious facts which have to be faced and I see no other way to deal with the matter. Simply to attempt to make it appear that there is no serious problem is not to face up to the facts at all.
We face another problem which may have an even more serious effect on the mining industry of British Columbia. Over the last few days it has been pointed out that the copper mines are in a very serious predicament. If the United States should go ahead with its proposal to impose a higher tariff on lead and zinc our mining industry will be almost wiped out. Something must be done in that regard. The government will have to take a stronger and firmer position with the United States authorities to make sure that nothing will be done that will put us in the position of having to try to export lead and zinc to the United States market in the face of a tariff rate that will be prohibitive.
While no action was taken by the last congress, it is quite obvious that strong forces are at work, and I believe that only today hearings began again in the United States and the lead and zinc producers of that country will be coming forward with very strong arguments. There is every danger that before long, probably by the first of the year, higher tariffs will be imposed unless the federal government takes very strong action to prevent it.
Since there is no further stockpiling in the United States it is obvious that necessarily there will have to be some curtailments of production, but the United States economy requires large amounts of imports from other countries, particularly from Canada. It is realized by Canadian producers that they will have to reduce the amount of their production and, so far as lead and zinc are concerned, the very large company with which I am more familiar has reduced its tonnage by some 20,000 tons over the past few months. They are playing their part.
It is up to the government to face up to these issues and do what they consider necessary. If necessary, they should continue this session on into the new year, but let us have something done that will provide for the unemployed by putting them to work. Then, too, let us hear that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) is going to do something about increasing the benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act for those who will have to maintain their families during this winter on the meagre amount that is allotted.

Actually, Mr. Speaker, I am a little bit hazy as to just what subject matter the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) raised. However, I believe what I wish to say is related, at least in part, to the matter he raised. I took it that he started his grievance from the point of objecting to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) suggesting that we in this house were somehow doing a disfavour to the Canadian people if we attempted to bring before the house a true report of the conditions existing in the parts of Canada from which we come, in respect to unemployment or other related matters. Certainly, on that point I find myself in agreement with the hon. member for Kootenay East.
I noticed that he started out by suggesting that the Prime Minister had taken a different view when he was in opposition. I am not particularly concerned about that quarrel between the hon. member for Kootenay East and the Prime Minister, now that the hon. member for Kootenay East finds himself on the opposite side of the house. However, I certainly consider that it was a little improper for the Prime Minister, when no more had been said than has been said in this house about some of the symptoms of unemployment that are arising in this country, to make the suggestion that we should, in effect, "pipe down" and not report to the house conditions as we find them.
In my own constituency, for example, I know that one of the large logging and forest products companies recently announced the closure of seven of its logging camps. I know that there are several hundred plywood workers in British Columbia who have recently been laid off because of a lack of orders for plywood products. Actually I do not know whether or not the hon. member for Kootenay East would agree with me, but I believe the real grievance we have to bring forward is a grievance on behalf of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr). So far as I can see this government is doing exactly what the previous administration did. They are putting the Minister of Labour out on a limb by expecting him to shoulder the whole burden of dealing with the various questions that relate to unemployment as they arise from time to time. I would suggest, therefore, that the Minister of Labour is really the person who has the legitimate grievance in this connection. I realize that being a member of the government he cannot speak for himself in this connection in the house, so I am sure he will appreciate it if one or two of the members on this side speak for him.

We understand, of course, that within his own jurisdiction the Minister of Labour does have the authority to introduce amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Several of us have suggested that this might be an appropriate time for him to do so. We realize that under the unemployment insurance commission comes the operation of the national employment service. I, for one, have already expressed some dissatisfaction over the fact that apparently all the Minister of Labour has done in connection with the national employment service is to issue some sort of a directive. He has been very hazy to date as to what results may have been achieved as a result of the issuance of this directive. I would suggest that if the operation of the national employment service is going to be more effective in this country than it has been in the past it requires much more than a directive. For one thing, there will have to be a great deal more use made of it by many of the large employers in this country than has been the case up until now.
There has been, I feel, a tendency on the part of many of these large employers to go to the national employment service when they are seeking workers with certain specialized skills. The practice throughout Canada as a whole, which I feel is all too prevalent, is for many of these employers to pick up their new employees from the line at the plant gate whenever they have an opportunity of doing that in periods of slack employment.
I would suggest that this matter of unemployment, when it arises, is really one for the concern and attention of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), as well as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), and that it is not altogether fair for people like the Minister of Finance to leave the Minister of Labour on his own to cope with unemployment problems. As the hon. member for Kootenay East was speaking, I recalled that when we were engaged in the debate on the last budget introduced in this house some of the problems which are coming to the fore today were brought out in discussion by some of the members. I said something in that connection myself at that time.
When one recognizes, as those of us who come from British Columbia do, that this winter is going to be a rather gloomy one for a good many of our constituents who are not going to be able to find work, we cannot but recall that during the last budget debate a great deal of the discussion centred around the inflationary pressures on the economy and upon the tremendous construction boom. So far as I am concerned, the situation that now is developing in the province of British
Unemployment
Columbia, according to all reports, is something for which the provincial administration has to take a great deal of the responsibility. During the budget debate I made some reference to the last budget speech in the provincial legislature by the minister of finance, Mr. Bennett. I had this to say, as recorded on page 2580 of Hansard for March 21, 1957:
As far as he can see,-
That is Mr. Bennett.

the only solution seems to be to go on spending and spending in the field of capital construction without giving any thought to what may happen if that capital spending should stop.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we are now beginning to see what some of the results are in the economy of British Columbia when the period arrives when this extremely rapid capital expenditure begins to slow down. I went on to say this:
When he talks about industry adjusting from time to time and taking the steps necessary for the consolidation of gains, the only meaning I can take from that is that sooner or later industry is going to stop this rapid expansion of plant and equipment.
Once that is done, then some of these thousands of people who have been attracted to our province may not be such welcome citizens as they are at the present time.
I made those remarks on March 21 of this year and they will be found at page 2580 of Hansard of that day. That is not very long ago. Yet already, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that some of the possibilities that I suggested then are coming to pass within our province. It should be of real concern to the members of this house that this is taking place. Undoubtedly and quite legitimately it should be brought to the attention of the government at this time.
The major industry in the Comox-Alberni area is, of course, the forest products industry. In that speech to which I have made reference I had something to say about conditions in the lumber industry. I pointed out that the great lumber corporations of the Pacific coast had over a period of years been able to make tremendous profits, a large part of which they had been plowing back into an expansion of the industry and into production facilities. In this connection I said on March 21:
Sooner or later this program of rapid capital expansion will have to come to an end, and when that happens, particularly if it should be that the existing market has temporarily or permanently declined, then our province is going to be in a very grave situation, and many thousands of workers who have been working at what, compared with the national average, are quite good wages, are no longer going to have that sort of job.
Mr. Speaker, I think that enough may have been said in the house, and certainly enough

Unemployment
press reports are appearing to demonstrate that the fears, if you want to call them that, which I expressed last March are actually becoming the realities of the situation as it currently exists in the province of British Columbia. In that speech I also suggested the possibility that a time would come when we would have built more pulp mills than necessary having regard to the amount of pulp we could sell and that when that situation developed we were going to have these various concerns competing for a larger share of an existing market or a contracting market, a situation which would result in instability of employment and in some of the lay-offs that in point of fact we are now experiencing in the province of British Columbia.
I think it is and would be ill-advised action on the part of anyone having the responsibility of government or of anyone supporting the government to suggest that when a member of parliament rises in his place and attempts to draw this situation to the attention of the house he is thereby being an alarmist, or is crying "blue ruin" or that by so doing he is aggravating the situation. As the hon. member for Kootenay East suggested, the Prime Minister on former occasions put into words the idea that if we do not rise in our places here and speak the facts we are deluding ourselves and are doing a disservice to the Canadian people. What else are we here for, Mr. Speaker, than to bring to the attention of the government, which has at any particular time the responsibility of looking after the welfare of this country, the facts of the situation as we see them?
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, as I said previously, I really feel that in rising to speak on the grievance raised by the hon. member for Kootenay East in this context I am really speaking on behalf of the Minister of Labour to his colleagues in the cabinet and asking them not to leave him out on a limb to cope single-handed with the solution of some of the problems that obviously are not entirely within his jurisdiction.

Mr. Speaker, I have a grievance and it is related to this question of unemployment. We are well aware of the fact that one of the first immediate things that was done by the government was to see to it that $150 million was provided for the purpose of constructing low-price homes. At the present time approximately $130 million of that sum of money has been allocated for that purpose and the government has intimated that when further moneys are required they will be made available. That particular effort on the part of the government was commendable and no

doubt as time goes on a great deal of additional money will be required.
At the present time we are fully aware of the fact that there are in this country about 250,000 unemployed people. Various estimates are given and it is suggested that the number of those unemployed could rise to half a million or three quarters of a million this winter. In our own province of British Columbia the number of unemployed persons has doubled as compared to the number one year ago. That situation today applies in the Okanagan Boundary area from which I come where we have a number of industries such as mining, logging, ranching, fruit growing and others and where people at this particular time of the year are faced with the problem of seasonal unemployment.
I have heard various members of this parliament suggest that the government should face up to this situation. I suggest that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) has a very difficult problem in this matter of unemployment and that if we, as members of parliament, can make suggestions to him, so much the better. However, thus far, after sitting in this house during the last five weeks, I have heard hardly any suggestions made for the purpose of minimizing the problems of the Minister of Labour. I should like to suggest that the federal government initiate an all-Canada work project.
At the present time the situation is favourable for that project because I believe that on November 25 and November 26 of this year there is to be a meeting between the various officials of the federal government and the premiers of the various provinces of Canada. I am more particularly concerned at the present time with those men in our country who are in destitute circumstances. What is going to be done in the next six months, twelve months or eighteen months to help those men who, through no fault of their own, cannot find employment? As you know, Mr. Speaker, unemployment is not a good thing for the country. It leads to increased crime. It means a waste of manpower. Not only that, but men who are not working suffer both mentally and physically.
I would suggest that the federal government initiate a works project and that men who are in destitute circumstances be given the opportunity to work on roads, to work on parks, to work on bridges and to work wherever they can serve a useful purpose for the country. It might be that when the government gives consideration to this matter it will say that these men who are in destitute circumstances should be paid a sum of money by way of a wage that is slightly in excess of the average amount paid to

people who receive unemployment benefit. That would, indeed, be a great step forward. As the house knows, in times of war and national disaster there is never any trouble about getting money, and in this time of peace, when we have in our midst people who are in poor circumstances financially I think the least we could do is to look after our own citizens and give them employment.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with my fellow members in the Social Credit party in stressing the urgency of alleviating the serious and growing unemployment situation in Canada. I should also like to point out the necessity of creating conditions in which all these willing and able people in our great country will have ample opportunity of finding gainful employment. The question arises: what does this new government intend to do with respect to this serious situation? It is a basic question, since we have heard no statement from the government with respect to what their plans are, and there is no suggestion in the speech from the throne that they have an answer to this problem.
Across this country unemployment and lay-offs are growing alarmingly. Being broke, hitting the financial bottom, being without work, are situations which confront hundreds of thousands of our people at this very moment. I can understand their feelings of anger; I can sense their feeling of unhappiness as they wait impatiently for some exercise of judgment with respect to solving the difficulties which face them. Unemployment involves more than human tragedies, it involves a very serious loss of production for our country, because unemployment is never isolated, it is felt right across the board of our economic life. So, we repeat: what does this Conservative government intend to do with respect to this very serious situation? Responsible leaders and economists have predicted that this winter may see the greatest number of unemployed in postwar years. To substantiate this claim, I refer to a memorandum to the government of Canada dated October 21, 1957 issued by the Canadian Labour Congress, where on page 6 the following appears:
The economic situation is causing us some anxiety. The August figure of persons without jobs and seeking work was 174,000. This is almost 69 per cent higher than last year. Even allowing for the increase in the total supply of workers available for work, unemployment in August was almost 64 per cent worse than last year. And the position is getting steadily worse. June this year was 31 per cent worse than June 1956; July was almost 55 per cent worse than 1956, August almost 64 per cent. There is every indication that September will be even worse.
Unemployment
The proportion of unemployed to the labour supply in August was still not very high. But August is always one of the lowest months of the year for unemployment. With this big increase in the summer, what will unemployment be like at the peak next March?
From August 1956 to March 1957, the number of persons without jobs and seeking work rose by 240,000. The same absolute increase this year would mean a March 1958 total of 414,000. But we shall be agreeably surprised if the figure is not considerably higher, unless the present trend is arrested or reversed. A very much smaller percentage increase than took place last year would bring the March 1958 figure up to the postwar peak of 9.5 per cent of the total number of workers. This winter may well see the worst unemployment since the war, perhaps as high as 450,000 persons without jobs and seeking work, and 700,000 unplaced applicants at N.E.S. offices.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I hope that those predictions are wrong. Nevertheless, there are several things, historical and economic, which bear repeating because they are true. I want to say this at the outset: I am not critical for the sake of being critical, but I say what I am going to say in order to emphasize the need of correcting this persistent problem seriously. What are the facts? During every session of parliament in the past the question of mass unemployment has been debated and discussed thoroughly. The answer, as presented in the case of the Social Credit party, involves the government's monetary and fiscal policies. By its very nature, unemployment involves monetary considerations. The federal government alone possesses the right of monetary correction. That is why we stand for, and demand, a new financial deal for Canadians.
The former Liberal government kept putting off the solution. Instead of action they adopted the attitude of letting the years bring what they may. Today we are again debating the unemployment situation. We deeply regret that the spokesmen for the new government seem to be meeting that situation in exactly the same manner as the previous administration. The same pattern appears. The only difference, as far as I have been able to see, is that on the one hand the Liberals openly mourn their loss of power, while on the other the new Conservative government has difficulty in constraining itself from showing its jubilation at being in power.
Unless the government announces without delay a new and dynamic monetary policy to meet the problem our suspicion will be confirmed that both the old-line parties have failed to devise policies which will create those conditions which I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks, namely conditions in which all our peoples will be able to find gainful employment.
I think it is a very sad commentary on the intelligence of this and previous administrations when we consider that when it comes to war or preparation for war they can use

Unemployment
the techniques of finance to accomplish what is virtually impossible, yet as soon as the emergency is over we find the paradox of poverty in the midst of plenty, the paradox of our people having produced abundance of goods and services and then being unable, through lack of purchasing power, to acquire what they have been able to produce.
I admit that the problem of unemployment is not a simple one and it is equally true that the solution lies not only in increased production but in a greater consumption of our goods both here and abroad. Referring specifically to the domestic field, it is obvious that we need financial policies which will more equitably equate the earning power of our people with the productive capacity of the nation. At the present time our gross national product is well over the $30 billion mark, yet the total of all purchasing power in our country is many billions of dollars less. The claim is made that unemployment is seasonable, that it is unavoidable and normal. That is one of the phony arguments that has been used by the two old line parties as an escape clause because they have not got an answer.
What is your answer?
I will tell you right away.
Let us have it.
You will learn in a while.

Our answer, Mr. Speaker, as I indicated before, is to make sure we reform our economic system and equate the purchasing power of our people with the productive power of this nation. We believe that parliament should have the power to determine a financial policy that will make it-
What have we got now?

-obligatory for the banking system of this country to monetize the real wealth produced by the people of Canada so that the total income of our people will automatically be sufficient to equal the total market value of their production. That is our answer.
What is wrong with that?
What is right about it?
The fact that you smile about it, that is what is wrong with it.

With respect to whether or not unemployment is normal I would say the only thing normal about unemployment in a country such as Canada is that it is a normal consequence of faulty monetary policy condoned by the old line parties.
(Mr. Holowach.]
Let us look at the facts. Across this country homes are desperately needed. We are falling further behind in the job of providing Canadians with decent and low-cost homes. Let us face up to the fact that shortages in housing are causing many crises in family life. Just how stupid can we be? We have the unemployed manpower, the materials and the skills to fulfil the housing needs but under the prevailing tight money policies of the previous Liberal administration as well as the new Conservative government home starts are dropping sharply and layoffs in all fields of the construction industry are on the increase.
Roads and arterial highways are desperately needed across the country. Some 16 years ago we commenced constructing the trans-Canada highway, one single road across the nation and it is still in process of being completed today. How long do we have to wait before we start to build the other highways that are essential to the economy and defence of Canada? On repeated occasions I have drawn the attention of the government to the need of constructing additional trans-Canada highways and in particular a highway that would run from Winnipeg by way of Saskatoon, Edmonton, Jasper park and the Yellowhead route to the west coast. It is about time we did something in that regard.
Right across Canada there is the need of vast national undertakings and projects essential to the national interest which are physically possible and desirable. Let us consider for a moment the backlog of essential public facilities at the junior or municipal level of government. This backlog includes hospitals to restore the health of our people, schools to relieve the shortage of classrooms and sewerage and sanitation projects to meet the requirements of expanding communities. In the light of these needs it is nonsense to suggest that unemployment in Canada is unavoidable or inevitable. In fact the most amazing spectacle in our country today is that of underemployment.
May we ask this question: will this government which prides itself on being a new deal government possess the courage to implement fiscal policies which in their objectives will aim to make financially possible what we know is physically possible and desirable? If we are able to do this Canada can be built into a leading nation within our lifetime. The remedy calls for a full recognition of the role of comsumption in our economic system. If this is so, then we must overhaul our tax structure which has reached excessive and crushing proportions and is destroying

the buying power of the dollar as related to the consumption of goods. The government must also help in meeting the credit and mortgage needs of our people in order that they may acquire homes at reasonable terms. Furthermore, the needs of small and mediumsized businesses must be recognized by reducing the crushing tax load and loan restrictions which face them. These are the shots in the arm which our country needs if we are to expand production and alleviate unemployment.
In this discussion of labour and unemployment problems I feel strongly there is one problem perhaps more worthy of our attention than any other. I have in mind the problem of older people seeking work and the difficulties they encounter in this connection. These difficulties are compounded not only by the barriers that are set up against them in industry but also by the neglect in legislation. Many of these older people are healthy and active but because of their age the opportunity to earn is denied them. Whether business is good or bad no one wants to hire the older worker.	Finding a solution to
this important problem of jobs for older people is a task for parliament, for industry and for the Department of Labour.
As a start I suggest the establishment of a fund and the institution of a program in the Department of Labour to help these people in the meantime by inducing priority in placement and to reduce the barriers erected against this worthy element of our society. I believe that to do this little bit is to do something that would at least give all of us a sense that we are participating in a positive action against manpower wastage as well as	one of special humanitarian
significance.
Mr. Speaker, I would not have the opposition feel that a member of the government party did not have a grievance with the government.
We are sure that yours will.

What I have to raise is a grievance which I think affects every constituency but perhaps I may apply my particular reference to the area I know best if the house will grant me that liberty. I intend in a very few words to make reference to air regulations and bilateral agreements but not necessarily to air carriers. My grievance is, if I may state it at the beginning, the lack of proper consideration for Canadian landing points which of course are subject to the international bilateral agreements. I do not blame Trans-Canada Air Lines; in fact
Air Transport
I think I might even pay them a compliment to a certain extent. We have heard on a number of occasions in this house severe criticism of Trans-Canada Air Lines and even the question of its proposed sale has been raised, with which view I do not agree. As an active pilot and one who has flown on most airlines on this continent I would say that in so far as aircraft servicing and airline practices are concerned there is no finer airline in the world, bar none.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I do agree with those who believe that it suffers from a rather sheltered position; and which very seriously affects its public relations.
In a paragraph or two I should like to urge upon the government the necessity of giving consideration to the problem of a number of communities which today are not serviced by any north-south connection and which, by their very nature, as I said initially, is regulated under the bilateral agreement and are influenced by what we regard as the cat-and-mouse game. The fact of the matter, Mr. Speaker, is that if you wish to initiate any possible landing right in one country or another you find that it involves a rather complicated agreement. The situation in Calgary is such-in fact, in the entire western area between Winnipeg and Vancouver- that we are not serviced to our southern cousins by anything other than one milk route. The net result is that a passenger- and there are a great many of them-who uses the south connection, such as it is, is forced to undergo a very lengthy layoff in one of two cities. In fact, it is nearly as fast to go by motor car or mule.
We in Calgary are in this position, and since it is applicable to a number of other centres, I would suggest that consideration be given to inviting the United States to reopen negotiations which admittedly have to date been conducted on a rather horsetrading basis in the past. I suggest that we point out to them that very large metropolitan centres are being denied free access by either Canadian or United States carriers. I am not concerned what carrier it might be purely because we are frightened to sit down around the negotiation table for fear that what we might gain on the one hand we would give away on the other. In the meantime those who are in the less populated areas have not the same influence and they suffer disastrously.
The city of Calgary is an example. It is a metropolitan centre which is naturally

Broadcasting Service
the headquarters of the oil industry. Because of the location of Calgary those personnel who wish to visit United States centres of industrial importance must go through Calgary. We have no airline route which would conceivably get them there directly unless they go into the city of Edmonton and take the northern route, or unless they take the bus in many instances and go to Lethbridge. It is interesting to note that 80 per cent of loadings for U.S. points from Alberta originate in Calgary, yet we have no service south. The net result is we have built up in the city of Calgary one of the biggest centres of private aviation of executive type aircraft that it is possible to have. Unfortunately, many of those people cannot afford this luxury and they have no hope of carrying out their business in an effective manner.
Therefore, my grievance, simply expressed, is this. Let us recognize that we are going to have to re-open the bilateral negotiations soon. Let us say that we are prepared to recognize that many of those areas-and particularly the constituency which I represent-have no service at all. Let us say to the United States that one of two carriers -two in particular in the United States- who are prepared to service Calgary should be permitted to come in unless some Canadian airline is permitted to give the same service. I hope, sir, that the government will consider this as a grievance because the problem is perhaps one of those which, from a convenience standpoint, is certainly most urgent.

REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF BROADCASTING SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a grievance to put before the house. With your permission I would like to speak about radio and television service more particularly as it concerns the area which I represent in this house the constituency of Chapleau.
A number of listeners in the Abitibi area have expressed the wish to be provided with certain religious broadcasts such as Sunday mass and morning devotions at 7.30 each morning, through the private stations at La Sarre and Amos.
Radio is a social service which should satisfy the tastes and the needs of the public. As the people of Abitibi are 90 per cent French-speaking and Catholic, it would be well for the C.B.C. to insist that the private stations associated with the government network, such as those of the Radio-Nord Inc.

chain, provide their listeners with a good many additional broadcasts originating with the C.B.C. I make that suggestion also on behalf of listeners who are in poor health, old, crippled, or invalids. I know too that a great many people who have to look after numerous small children are unable to attend mass every Sunday because of the distance they live from the churches.
My request is also justified by section 21 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act (chapter 32 RSC). The broadcasting licences are defined as being a temporary and conditional alienation of an important and precious element of public wealth to the benefit of a group or a company.
The C.B.C. is empowered to set the periods during which a private station must carry network programs. Licence holders, especially those in private networks, who are thereby the sole broadcasters in an isolated area such as ours, have a duty to supply to the whole of their listening public the best programs of the French network.
As regards the radio program called "Morning Devotions", it is so varied and of such high quality that our people would like to enjoy it every day. It must not be replaced by songs or by music sometimes of a dubious if not bad taste. Would you agree, Mr. Speaker, to replace the daily prayer in the house by discussions relating to rock'n roll? Certainly not.
Private radio stations should at all times show themselves worthy of the licence that has been granted to them, and of the privilege of the exclusive use of the air, which is part of public property.
An effective way for the government to encourage a better standard of radio service in a given area consists in supplying that area with the additional service of the C.B.C., thereby giving listeners the opportunity to choose whichever program they prefer.
I favour private enterprise as long as it maintains for the benefit of the public a service always worthy of commendation.
I would like to add a few words, if I may, on a related subject. I assure you that, in the Abitibi area, we have long wanted to view the programs which the French television network has been broadcasting for the past five years in Canada. According to official reports supplied to us, 86 p. 100 of this country is now well covered in this field. We should like to have the same treatment in

the Chapleau constituency. We should like the advantages of French television service because this service would only be normal, I believe, in an area where the population is almost 90 p. 100 French-speaking. It is only fair to ask the government to offer us at least the French programs if it is too difficult to give us the benefit of both networks as is already the case for many other areas.
A private station, CKRN - TV in our neighbouring county of Villeneuve, should soon start its TV operations but will not cover the whole of my area. For that reason, I ask the government to supply us with the services of the national network in Chapleau. At Rouyn, in the county of Villeneuve, CKRN - TV will assign 50 p. 100 of its time to French programs. But this is not enough. What we want is a transmitting station for the benefit of the eastern part of Chapleau, Barraute, to Clova and Parent, an area more than 200 miles long which will not be reached by the Rouyn station.
Everywhere in Canada, the population insists on getting numerous programs of an irreproachable quality. People who know have said that C.B.C. compares favourably with other richer and more extensive networks. Canadians may no doubt be proud of the C.B.C., and it is exactly because we are 125,000 Canadians proud of the progress made by our country that we insist and wish to see, in our own homes, with our own eyes, the gigantic growth of Canada through the medium of radio and television. We need a service of this type for our entertainment but still more, no doubt, for education purposes. We need television, for instance, for all our bush workers and our mine workers who live very far from the cities and have no other means than radio to witness the gigantic growth of our country. We must open a window to children and our fellow citizens so that they may know each other better and have more reason to love Canada, a country of more than 16J millions of citizens who should have closer relations in order to achieve their goal, that is to live in good understanding, from one part of the country to the other.
To reach that goal, Mr. Speaker, it would be as necessary to supply all our fellow citizens with adequate radio and television services as to defend ourselves from external enemies who sometimes spread subversive propaganda.
Broadcasting Service
We recognize that our radar systems of warning, those for example of Parent and Senneterre, which have been set up at great cost, are useful even if one day we find that guided missiles could fall on us before the signal is given by telephone to the prime minister's office.
And as far as we are concerned, Mr. Speaker, we believe that the requested radio and TV service is as urgent and more important, for several reasons, than the broadcast of numerous international programs in sixteen or seventeen foreign languages to serve the Norwegians, the Swedes, the Danes, the Finns, the Dutch, the Italians, the Germans, the Austrians, the Czechs, the Russians, the Ukrainians, the Poles or others. It would be more urgent to offer this service to the French Canadians of northwestern Quebec who have none at all than to the peoples of Europe or Latin America who do not pay any taxes in Canada. Canadians have to pay for that. May the government then give, without any more delay, complete broadcast service in French or in the two languages so recently spoken by our very gracious sovereign, Her Majesty the Queen, when she visited Ottawa.
Admittedly the government finances an important part of television. Such being the case we would like the C.B.C. to set aside a part of the money it receives to create a system of relay towers which would bring T.V., by microwave over the Laurentians, beginning at Ottawa or Montreal, and reaching northward as far as the constituency of Chapleau. This should be done even at the expense of reducing broadcasts beamed towards Europe.
Let the C.B.C. create a high power station to serve Canadians in Chapleau. Some of the larger centres enjoy the two networks at the same time, which is all to the good. But, Mr. Speaker, we would at least like to have French language television service throughout our home area. I could add at this point that my constituents have already begun, in large numbers, to pay towards the cost of establishing such a telecommunication service by buying receiving sets which are liable to a special 15 per cent sales' tax the proceeds of which are handed over to the C.B.C. which uses them to establish new services.
If the government were to decide that the development in question would cost the C.B.C. too much at this time, do not forget that it would be in a better position to justify the maintenance costs of the radar system passing through Parent, Senneterre, and along the "Pinetree" line, if a picture transmission service were added to the latter. If the government really wishes to economize as claimed,

Broadcasting Service
it would be easy for the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes), the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) who has the C.B.C. in his care, and the other members of the government, to direct that the "Pine-tree" radar line be modified to transmit television pictures as far as Parent and Senne-terre, where radar stations are located and enable our people to receive the telecasts thus relayed. Some say that our defence and radio and television services are more or less kept in watertight compartments. Well, those are the very compartments which the government must open. Let us therefore hold a conference at the Parent station or, if it is preferable, at Senneterre, where the Gordian knot could easily be cut.
On behalf of all the people of my constituency, I therefore urge the federal government to take immediate action to achieve in the near future the two improvement and development suggestions which I have explained too rapidly here concerning radio and television broadcasting, particularly in the eastern part of my constituency.
After witnessing several days ago all that was done in order that our royal visitors could appear at the same time on the Canadian and American television networks, I am sure that, if the government will only give favourable consideration to our requests, everything will be in operation very shortly.
In a few weeks the C.B.C. has done wonders, and I commend those who have directly or indirectly taken part in this gigantic operation, which made it possible for us to see Her Majesty the Queen of Canada, and thus admire and respect her the more.
Unfortunately, the children of my district have, generally speaking, not been able to see Queen Elizabeth. We should not wait any longer; it is time to act and the whole population of Chapleau is anxious to see this project carried out.
It is true that the networks have cost many million dollars last year; five million people have seen live broadcasts of our great hockey games. And, as soon as the winter season begins, we, in my riding of Chapleau and elsewhere, also want to see all the hockey games and all the educational programs, which the C.B.C. may broadcast every day. The project is feasible, if the government really wants to give us the improvements I request and which the people of my county of Chapleau entirely approve.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my grievance is the same one in principle as that of the previous speaker but

with a different locale. I rise to protest the continued denial of satisfactory radio reception to some 5,000 of my constituents and the denial to those constituents of the opportunity to hear the excellent programs of the C.B.C. We have had radio operations in Canada for over 30 years. One would hardly credit that in one constituency there are over 5,000 people today who have not had the opportunity to enjoy the programs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation except on very rare occasions in daylight hours. During the evenings they have to rely entirely upon United States programs which many of them do not enjoy to any great extent.
I speak from personal experience, Mr. Speaker, because my little log cabin is situated in this considerable area that is isolated from the general communications of the C.B.C. To show how difficult it is, I remember that one Sunday evening one of my daughters came and said, "The member for Macleod is speaking, daddy." We twiddled with the radio and could hear a squeak and a burp and finally we heard a voice say, "This is San Francisco; you have been listening to Charlie McCarthy." Anyway, Mr. Speaker, that is the sort of radio reception we get in our district. I know the department concerned and the C.B.C. have been interested in correcting this situation for some years. Some years ago studies were made with respect to installing a somewhat higher powered station somewhere in the interior of British Columbia. After various tests were made, it was found that even the expenditure of quite a large sum of money would not guarantee satisfactory radio reception to the area in my constituency to which I am referring. I understand from the engineers and technicians that this difficulty is caused by the mountainous terrain and the very small amount of soil over a large section of the mountains themselves at the higher levels. I understand it is a condition that also exists in some other parts of Canada.
Anyway when that was discovered I was informed the only way to correct this situation and bring the programs of the C.B.C. to these 5,000 people denied them was to go in for the erection of low-power relay stations. Naturally, I was all for that suggestion. I have been urging that for some seven years in this house, Mr. Speaker. We required some five stations, I understand, to satisfactorily serve the areas particularly mentioned. We had two stations installed, one at Castle-gar and one at Kaslo. The one at Kaslo serves a population which is delighted to

have the opportunity of listening to the C.B.C. and other Canadian programs. Naturally, this improved radio reception at Kaslo has caused an increasing ferment amongst those who have been denied radio reception for a period of 30 years, while at the same time we are spending many millions on bringing television to the majority of the Canadian people.
This situation is of such concern to these constituents of mine that the farmers' institutes, women's institutes, chambers of commerce, boards of trade and other organizations have dealt with the question at various meetings and have adopted resolutions and forwarded them to me as well as to the appropriate persons in the various government departments. In addition to that, at the last convention of the chambers of commerce of southeastern British Columbia a resolution was again passed asking the government to give consideration to the correction of the situation so far as radio reception is concerned in those areas of southeastern British Columbia denied it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, after we had the two stations installed, the one at Castlegar and the one at Kaslo-which incidentally is the birthplace, I believe, of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) and I know he is interested in this question so I expect him to support me on it-I have been informed that the others could not be erected because of a lack of funds and the expense in developing television. In order to service the district properly a low-power relay station should be erected at Balfour to serve the Kootenay lake area and the communities of Queens Bay, Kootenay Bay, Proctor, Crawford Bay, Gray Creek, Port Crawford and Boswell. There should be another one erected on Slocan lake, possibly at Roseberry. There is one required at Nakusp to serve the Upper Arrow lakes and south.
As I said before, I have urged the installation of these stations for seven years, then suddenly we were faced with the fact that there was insufficient funds owing to the increased expenditures of the C.B.C. on the extension of radio and television in other areas, but particularly with respect to television. Then I was told the matter would have to lay in abeyance until the report of the royal commission on broadcasting and television was received. Well, Mr. Speaker, that commission reported this year, March 15, and in its report dealt with this very important question. I have made many representations in this house and the matter has been brought to the attention of the special committee on broadcasting and television on several occasions. I had considerable correspondence 96698-84
Broadcasting Service
with the various ministers, the governor of the C.B.C. and his technical and engineering Staff in British Columbia. I hope we are getting much closer to the time when the situation I have mentioned will be corrected.
I want to quote for a few minutes from the report because it mentions that this is a situation that has been experienced by other communities in Canada and certainly it should not be allowed to continue in this day and age. There is a chapter in this book entitled "Improvement and Extension of Coverage". I am quoting from the report of the royal commission on broadcasting, 1957, and this is what is stated at page 209:
It came as something of a surprise to us that as much as 74 per cent of our total population is within reach of four or more radio stations during the daytime. At night, this percentage drops to about 43 per cent due to an increase in interference from distant co-channel and adjacent channel stations. The following table shows the percentages of population capable of hearing one, two, three or four or more Canadian radio stations.
At first glance, it would appear that radio coverage in Canada is very good. And indeed it is. Yet there are still almost half a million people in this country who cannot, except under freak atmospheric conditions, receive the signal of even one Canadian station. After considering every aspect of this question with our financial advisers and the C.B.C. management, we have come to the conclusion that a limited plan for the extension of radio coverage is desirable.
Then, at page 210 the commission had this to say:
The most important single element in this plan is the erection of the 97 low-power relay transmitters and the four new transmitters which is contemplated in our six-year forecast at a total capital cost of nearly $2 million. These new facilities, particularly the low-power relay transmitters, are to be located in remote areas of every province except Prince Edward Island which, for obvious reasons, does not give rise to as difficult problems as her sister provinces. The over-all capital investment in the extension plan will be about $3.3 million including a contingency of $1 million to provide for future growth and shifts in population.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do urge the government, when it is considering this report and preparing its estimates-I am now speaking to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), the Minister of Public Works for sympathetic purposes, and I trust the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) will read what I have to say tomorrow morning as he usually does- to give consideration to the fact that radio services should be rendered to these people who are producing a lot of wealth in the isolated portions of this country.
Incidentally, I might mention in this respect that I represent the constituency that pays the highest income tax per capita in Canada and has the highest wage income per capita in large sections of the constituency as a result of the operations of the smelter, mining industry and lumbering industry.

Beet Sugar Industry
This constituency makes quite a contribution to the national revenue, and on that basis and in view of all the circumstances and the fact it is working to pay its own share, I hope my representations will engender a favourable response from the ministers concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to voice a grievance in that the Canadian sugar industry appears to continue to be dangerously exposed to Cuban sugar producers. May I draw to the attention of the house a number of important facts concerning the beet sugar industry of Canada. The beet sugar industry does help, and could and would help Canada, first, to deal with her serious adverse trade balance problem; second, to ameliorate her wheat surplus problem; third, to make highly beneficial use of her fine irrigation districts in Alberta and elsewhere; fourth, to strengthen her supply position in case of war, particularly in reference to sugar for human food and for all its many other uses, as well as to certain extremely valuable livestock feeds including wet beet pulp, dried beet pulp, beet tops, beet molasses and beet tailings; fifth, to provide employment for many Canadians, and home markets for several Canadian products of which let me mention coal, coke, lime and bags, to list only a few; sixth, to conserve and enrich Canadian soils upon which the sugar beets are grown.
The beet growing industry is a thoroughly sound agricultural industry. It is just as sound as is any other branch of Canadian agriculture such as grain growing, poultry producing, dairying or livestock raising. The sugar beet growers, like the growers of any other product in Canada, are vulnerable to dangers within Canada such as factors like a cost-price squeeze. They are vulnerable also to unfair competition from outside Canada, factors like the cane sugar producers of Cuba, the Philippines and other tropical countries with low wage scales and exceptional climatic, geographical and other advantages, such exceptionally favoured cane producers, if unhindered by special Canadian restrictive measures, being, in any normal year, able to pour into Canada enough refined sugar to ruin Canadian sugar producers, either beet sugar growers and refiners, or cane refiners.
Canadian beet sugar refiners require the Canadian federal government's care, much as do other Canadian agricultural producers. Canadian beet sugar growers ought to be shielded by the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Canada's beet sugar producers ought to be secured by a Canadian sugar act appropriately like the United States sugar act

of 1948, which act is based upon (1) quotas, (2) price adjustments; (3) extensive home production of sugar consumption.
May I give the house a few facts to show something of what Cuba has done in times past, and what conceivably Cuba might do again; facts to show also what Canada did to protect her producers both of cane and of beet sugar? During the year 1931 the price of Cuban sugar fell to an almost unbelievably low level. Tariffs could not shut it out. Canada, on January 27, 1932, passed order in council P.C. 181, granting power of fixing, for duty purposes, at $2.30 per hundred weight the price of outside sugar at place of origin. On January 30 appraiser's bulletin No. 3815 announced this fixing of sugar price. This measure shut Cuban sugar out of Canada.
The Liberal government on November 20, 1939 cancelled, as a wartime move, appraiser's bulletin No. 3815. This action left the sugar controller of Canada to take whatever means he might consider needful to exclude, or to admit, sugar from outside Canada. The Liberal government abolished wartime control of sugar on April 1, 1950.
In 1952 Cuban sugar began coming into Canada in great amounts. Apparently Right Hon. C. D. Howe had a personal promise from Cuba that she would refrain from sending Cuban refined into Canada in injurious quantities.
Will the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) look into the situation at present and, at an early date, give the house a statement upon the whole situation as regards Canadian beet sugar producers and Cuban sugar? Then will he tell us whether or not there has been anything comparable to the imposition of the $2.30 minimum at place of origin? If nothing like that has been done, I feel that our producers are in a dangerous position.
Some hon. members will wonder whether or not all of the statements I have made in making these remarks can be adequately substantiated with dependable data and other evidence. Because of the shortage of time at my disposal I have had to omit the plentiful documentary and other evidence in my possession. Those desiring to read that evidence may find much of it in a speech which I delivered on December 4, 1952, as recorded on pages 339344, volume I of 1952-53 Hansard. They will find additional evidence in a speech which I delivered on December 17, 1952, as recorded on pages 840-845 in the same volume of Hansard. Still further evidence will be found in a speech I delivered on February 11, 1953, as recorded on pages 1841-1846 of 1952-53 Hansard; and yet more in my speeches of March 5, 1953, recorded on pages 2654-2659

and of March 16, 1953, as recorded on pages 2972-2976 of 1952-53 Hansard.
In my speech of April 7, 1953, recorded on pages 3560-3565 of 1952-53 Hansard is to be found a discussion of the United States sugar act of 1948, why it was enacted, and what it provides as a solution to the difficult problem of sugar in any country like Canada or the United States. The United States sugar act of 1948 has recently been extended indefinitely with modifications.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the minister that he give the most careful consideration to the drafting and introduction of a Canadian sugar act similar to that of the United States.
